report.tagline: A card and digital wallet that combines all your bank cards into one, so you can switch which card pays even after you have paid.
report.simpleSummary: Curve is one card that sits on top of all your other cards. You add your Barclays debit card, your Amex and your Monzo card to the Curve app, then pay with the Curve card or phone. Curve passes the payment to whichever card you choose. If you paid with the wrong card, you can move the payment to another card afterwards. Lloyds Banking Group bought Curve to use its wallet technology.

overview.whatItDoes: Curve is a Mastercard debit card and app that routes each payment to one of your existing cards. It adds features your bank cards may not have, like moving a past payment to a different card, lower fees abroad and cashback. It also offers Curve Pay, a tap-to-pay wallet on phones. In 2026 it became part of Lloyds Banking Group.
howItWorks: You add your existing debit and credit cards to the Curve app.
You pay with the Curve card, or Curve Pay on your phone, and choose which card is active.
Curve charges your chosen card for the same amount in the background.
'Go Back in Time' lets you move a past payment to another card within a set number of days.
Smart Rules can pick a card automatically, for example your credit card for anything over £100.
Paid plans add more free foreign exchange, cashback and extra features.
overview.valueProposition: Carry one card instead of many, always pay with the best card for each purchase, and fix mistakes after you have paid.

businessModel.summary: Curve made money from a small fee on each card payment, from foreign exchange fees above free limits, and from paid plan subscriptions. The problem: it often pays more to charge your underlying card than it earns on the Curve card, so the model is thin.

revenueStreams.detail: A small fee the shop's bank pays each time the Curve card is used.
Monthly fees for paid plans with more benefits.
Fees on foreign spending above free limits and on weekends.
Now mainly a technology asset inside Lloyds rather than a standalone business.

businessModel.pricing: Free plan with limited fee-free FX and features. Paid plans have ranged from a few pounds a month up to about £15 for the top tier with insurance and higher limits. Check the app for current plans.
costDrivers: Fees Curve pays when it charges your underlying card (especially credit cards and Amex)
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a £50 shop payment on Curve. Curve earns about 10p to 20p in interchange from the shop's side. Then it charges your credit card for £50, and that may cost Curve around 10p to 40p, because the card in the middle pays too. So Curve can make nothing or lose money on each payment. Subscriptions help, but most users stay on the free plan. That thin margin is why Curve struggled to grow profitably and ended up being sold to a bank.

howTheyGetUsers: Points and travel blogs that recommend Curve
whatBringsUsersBack: Using it for every payment once it is the default card
Go Back in Time to fix mistakes
growth.moat: Weak as a standalone. Card networks and Amex can limit how cards are used through Curve, and Apple and Google own the phone wallet. The technology and the Curve Pay wallet were valuable enough for Lloyds to buy, but the business model alone did not create a strong moat.

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Revolut holds your money; Curve sits on top of other cards.

competitors.name: Wise
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Wise is better for holding currencies; Curve is better for using existing cards.

competitors.name: Bank apps
competitors.positioning: Banks adding their own wallet and rewards features.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Curve works across banks; now it is part of one bank.

pmLessons: A great feature is not a business. Curve's product was loved but its revenue per payment was too thin.
Building on top of other companies' rails (card networks, Amex, Apple) means they can change the rules on you.
Sometimes the best outcome for a product is to become part of a bigger platform.
Check unit economics early: if each transaction loses money, more growth makes it worse.

interviewQuestions.question: Why did Curve struggle to become profitable?
interviewQuestions.hint: Walk through one payment: interchange earned vs cost to charge the underlying card. Add low paid conversion and platform dependence.

interviewQuestions.question: You are a PM at Lloyds after buying Curve. What do you build first?
interviewQuestions.hint: Pick the users (Lloyds customers on Android), the feature (wallet with Go Back in Time), and the metric (wallet payments). Explain trade-offs.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you increase Curve's paid plan conversion?
interviewQuestions.hint: Find which features users would pay for, like FX and insurance. Test pricing and trials. Measure conversion and churn.

interviewQuestions.question: Apple opened NFC access in the EU. What does that mean for Curve?
interviewQuestions.hint: It lets Curve Pay work on iPhone in the EU. Discuss reach, cost of building, and Apple's fees.

interviewQuestions.question: What north star metric would you pick for Curve?
interviewQuestions.hint: Payments per active user shows replacement of other cards. Compare with sign-ups or revenue.
